drills.q: Define image vs container precisely enough to survive a follow-up question.
drills.a: Image: read-only, content-addressed layers plus config JSON (entrypoint, env, ports). Container: that image plus one writable layer, plus namespaces (pid/net/mnt/uts/ipc/user) and cgroups enforcing resource limits.

drills.q: You reorder a Dockerfile so requirements.txt is copied and installed before COPY . ., but builds are still slow on every commit. What do you check next?
drills.a: Whether the build context itself is large and slow to hash/send due to a missing .dockerignore (pulling in .git, node_modules, a venv), or whether something upstream of the dependency install layer (like the base image tag) is actually changing on each build.

drills.q: A container exits immediately with exit code 0 but you expected a long-running server. Diagnose.
drills.a: Check docker logs for what actually ran, then the entrypoint/CMD itself -- a common bug is a script that backgrounds the server (server &) and then exits, taking PID 1 and the whole container down even though the backgrounded process was technically still alive from the shell's view.

drills.q: docker stats shows healthy memory usage right up until the container dies with exit 137. What's likely happening and how do you confirm the real cause?
drills.a: Page cache/buffer memory and short-lived allocation spikes (e.g. a GC pause building up garbage before collecting) can exceed the cgroup memory limit between docker stats polling intervals. Confirm via dmesg/kernel OOM logs for the actual kill event rather than trusting the last stats sample.

drills.q: You bind-mount your whole project directory, including node_modules built on macOS, into a Linux container. What breaks and why?
drills.a: Native binary dependencies (compiled node modules, some Python C extensions) built for the host OS/arch get shadowed into the container and won't run if the container's OS/arch differs. Fix: exclude node_modules/venv from the bind mount, install fresh inside the container.

drills.q: Two plain `docker run` containers can't resolve each other by name, but the same setup works under docker-compose up. Explain and fix without Compose.
drills.a: Embedded DNS (127.0.0.11) only works on user-defined bridge networks; the default bridge doesn't have it. Fix: docker network create mynet, run both containers with --network mynet.

drills.q: docker system df shows 40GB reclaimable in images but docker image prune -a only frees 5GB. Why the gap?
drills.a: prune -a still respects images referenced by any container (running or stopped) or tagged with something other than <none>. Check docker ps -a for stopped containers holding references that count as 'in use' even though nothing is actively running.

drills.q: Your app needs 25 seconds to drain in-flight requests on shutdown, but production shows connections cut off abruptly. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The default docker stop grace period (10s) is shorter than the app's drain time, so SIGKILL lands mid-drain. Fix: docker stop -t 30 (or the orchestrator equivalent, e.g. terminationGracePeriodSeconds in Kubernetes); confirm via exit code 137/forced-termination correlated with truncated connections at the deploy timestamp.

drills.q: docker build fails in CI with 'no space left on device' but works locally every time. Root cause and the durable fix, not just the quick one.
drills.a: CI runners reuse the same disk across builds without a developer's implicit periodic cleanup, so /var/lib/docker fills with unpruned layers. Quick fix is docker system prune -af; the durable fix is CI-native layer caching (BuildKit --cache-from/--cache-to against a registry) with an explicit size/TTL policy instead of relying on manual pruning.

drills.q: Explain why PID 1 inside a container needs special signal handling, and how a shell-wrapped CMD breaks it.
drills.a: PID 1 in a namespace gets no default signal handlers and must reap zombie children; without an explicit handler, SIGTERM is ignored until the grace period expires and SIGKILL lands. `CMD ["sh","-c","python app.py"]` makes the shell PID 1, so the signal never reaches the actual app process -- use exec form or `exec` inside the script.
